voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort are things to lay down in order to come near him. 

Paula wept at the manger. She greeted Bethlehem as the house of bread, where the Bread come down from heaven was born. To the virgin, Jesus is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the penitent, he is the doctor who receives the broken. To the scholar, he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

false_friend: "the Vulgate" as an already-standard, church-wide text (within this world's own span the project was ongoing, partial, and contested)

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
He entered the world as a poor child, born in Bethlehem in a feeding trough. He taught, and his teaching reached us in the writings we spent our lives correcting and translating. He died - and that death is our redemption. He rose from the dead, and that resurrection is the promise we gave up everything to follow.

More than three and a half centuries stood between us and those events. No one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as we received them, the unbroken worship of the churches, and - unusually for us - the places themselves. We could walk to the cave of the birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness, and our founders crossed the sea to live inside it.

What we had about him was first and above everything the writings - the Gospels and the whole of scripture, which we copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest, the Hebraica veritas.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
The truth kept in the Hebrew itself - we called it Hebraica veritas. It is the conviction that the Hebrew text of scripture is the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction drove the whole translation project. 

Jerome spent decades rendering the Hebrew into Latin, book by book, correcting against what he held to be the truer source. It was not an uncontested method. Augustine resisted it. Congregations resisted it. At one church in North Africa, a single changed word - "gourd" instead of "ivy" in the book of Jonah - caused such an uproar that the bishop nearly lost his see. But we held to it. For us, correcting a word against the Hebrew was as much a discipline as fasting. This was formation as textual asceticism. Renunciation and scriptural labor were one discipline, not two.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
We believed Jesus is the Word of God made flesh because that is the apostles' faith as the councils confessed it - Nicaea above all. We were born after that council. The faith came to us as the church's settled confession, not as a vote's invention. In our account, the council rejected a new teaching and confessed what the churches already worshipped.

But the shape our belief took - building our home beside the cave, giving away fortunes, Paula weeping at the manger - came from something else. We held that the Lord of all things entered the world poor, in a feeding trough. That poverty was not an accident of his birth. It was the pattern. Wealth, rank, and comfort became things to lay down in order to come near him. Jerome told a story against himself: in a dream he stood accused of following Cicero, not Christ, for where his treasure was, there his heart was also. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God. We believed because the apostles and councils handed it down. We believed the way we did because his poverty called us to our own.
